headlines.title: 49ers owner Jed York arrested in Ohio, pleads no contest to charges
headlines.description: San Francisco 49ers 49ers owner Jed York pleaded no contest to criminal charges Monday after being arrested on suspicion of engaging in prostitution in Ohio over the weekend, according to court records. York pleaded no contest to misdemeanor disorderly conduct and possessing criminal tools during a court appearance Monday morning. An administrative judge found him guilty following the plea and ordered him to pay just under $1,300 in fines and court costs. York was arrested by East Palestine police and booked into the Columbiana County Jail just after 10:40 a.m. Sunday, according to a jail official who spoke with NBC Bay Area. The jail official said York was originally booked on suspicion of engaging in prostitution and possessing criminal tools. The criminal tool in question was a cellphone, according to the official. York posted $5,000 bail and was released before 5 p.m. Sunday, according to the jail official. As part of Monday’s court proceedings, the judge ordered York’s cellphone returned to him. However, $160 in cash seized by police will be forfeited to the Mahoning Valley Human Trafficking Task Force, according to court records. The NFL issued a statement Monday following York’s arrest. “We are aware of the matter which will be reviewed under the personal conduct policy,” the league said. The 49ers also issued a statement Monday. “As this is a legal matter, which has been resolved, we will not be providing any further comment at this time,” the team said in a statement.

headlines.title: Newsom returns to a defining California fight: Who pays for wildfire damage?
headlines.description: The bookends of California Gov. Gavin Newsom’s nearly eight years in office have been defined by a crucial question: Who should cover the cost of damage from wildfires caused by utility equipment? The most destructive wildfire in state history, a blaze that killed 85 people and destroyed more than 18,000 buildings in Northern California, started two days after Newsom won the governorship in 2018. Investigators determined it was caused by Pacific Gas & Electric equipment. Facing tens of billions of dollars in liability, the giant utility filed for bankruptcy just weeks after Newsom’s inauguration. Months later, Newsom signed a law creating a $21 billion fund, paid for by utility shareholders and ratepayers, to help utilities pay for wildfire damages if they take certain safety measures. Now, as the final legislative session of his governorship ends, Newsom is trying to broker a deal with lawmakers aimed at further shielding utilities from financial trouble if their equipment sparks a wildfire. His push comes as another major utility, Southern California Edison, faces claims from the state’s second-most destructive blaze, a 2025 fire that killed 19 people outside of Los Angeles. Investigators ruled this month that it was sparked by one of the company’s transmission towers. Newsom’s plan could limit the amount electric and gas companies have to pay victims and attorneys. One of the goals is to stabilize the state’s electricity rates, which are among the highest in the nation and have continued to climb in recent years. Utilities have raised rates to pay for wildfire prevention and recovery as climate change has made the blazes more intense and frequent. Six of the state’s 10 most destructive wildfires have been caused by utility equipment. Newsom says the state needs to act quickly because he expects the wildfire fund to run out soon. His plan would require survivors to get paid by utilities sooner. “Status quo is not going to work,” Newsom recently told reporters. “It’s not going to work for victims, who consistently are last in line. And that’s at the core of this reform.” But some of those victims are pushing back. They’ve said Newsom’s plan prioritizes utilities over the needs of fire survivors. Meanwhile, insurance companies are concerned they would foot more of the bill for property damage. A coalition including the state’s major utilities — PG&E, Southern California Edison, and San Diego Gas & Electric — has been urging lawmakers to pass the plan. The last-minute legislative battle could help shape Newsom’s legacy as he considers a run for president in 2028. Newsom says his plan strikes a fair balance Under California law, utilities have to pay damages for fires ignited by their equipment, even if a judge doesn’t find them negligent. Home insurers that pay for policyholders’ rebuilding expenses can try to get reimbursed by utilities. Newsom’s plan could change that by making insurance companies cover more of the cost of property damage. The proposal would also require utility CEOs to forfeit bonuses if their company sparks a wildfire resulting in more than $1 billion worth of damage. And utility shareholders could be fined up to $10 million for violating wildfire prevention requirements, according to the governor’s office, which hasn’t released the full details. Personal Insurance Federation of California, a group representing property insurers across the state, said insurance rates will increase if the plan is implemented. The onus should remain on utilities to pay, said Rex Frazier, the federation’s president. “Being responsible for your actions is something that parents tell children,” he said in a statement. “Hopefully the Legislature will tell this to the utilities.” Fire survivors are also frustrated with the plan, which could limit their payouts. Joy Chen, executive director of Every Fire Survivor’s Network, a group of survivors of the 2025 Los Angeles-area fires, blasted it at a virtual town hall this month. “This is overall a massive transfer of liability for the three for-profit utility monopolies that have continued to burn down communities across California,” Chen said. The Legislature has until Aug. 31 to pass a plan. If they don’t, Newsom could call them back for a special session. Democratic legislative leaders say the state needs to address the issue but haven’t specified what a deal could include. Newsom proposed another $18 billion last year to supplement the wildfire fund, which the Legislature approved. An economist says the state should reduce utility liability California’s longstanding requirement that utilities cover the cost of wildfire damages regardless of whether they were negligent is based on the fact that they are providing a public service, said Meredith Fowlie, an economist who co-directs an energy institute at the University of California, Berkeley. But as climate change has fueled more frequent and destructive fires, the state should rethink how to distribute the ballooning costs of recovering from those blazes, she said. “Utilities can start fires, but they don’t by themselves create catastrophe,” Fowlie said. Other factors make wildfires turn into catastrophes, such as failing to clear vegetation or upgrade homes to make them more fire-resistant, she said. The question of who should be held responsible — and by how much — is “a critical, core issue that we have not dealt with and is not going away,” Fowlie said. Newsom says he’s prepared to tackle the issue he’s kept revisiting since he took office. “I’m not going to walk away and hand a real mess to the next governor,” he said last week.

headlines.title: Person shot, killed in Oakland
headlines.description: A person was killed in a shooting Monday morning in Oakland, according to police. Oakland police said officers responded just after 10:30 a.m. to a ShotSpotter activation in the 2000 block of 23rd Avenue. When officers arrived, they found a victim suffering from at least one apparent gunshot wound. The victim died at the scene, police said. The Oakland Police Department’s Homicide Section is investigating the circumstances surrounding the shooting. The victim’s identity is being withheld pending notification of next of kin. Police have not released information about a possible suspect or what may have led to the shooting. Anyone with information is asked to contact OPD’s Homicide Section at 510-238-3821 or the department’s tip line at 510-238-7950. Photos or videos related to the investigation can be sent to cidvideos@oaklandca.gov. This is a developing story. Please check back for updates.

headlines.title: 1 dead after fiery crash on I-580 in Livermore
headlines.description: A fatality was reported after a crash early Monday morning on Interstate Highway 580 in Livermore, according to the California Highway Patrol. Around 3:30 a.m., the CHP said it closed westbound I-580 near the southbound Livermore Avenue exit due to the crash. The lanes reopened around 5:15 a.m. There were no further details about the fatality immediately released.

headlines.title: Man arrested on suspicion of fatally shooting his brother in Fairfield
headlines.description: A man suspected of shooting and killing his brother in Fairfield on Saturday was arrested on Sunday on allegations of homicide. Christopher Cullen, 56, was detained following the shooting, which he allegedly reported himself. The Fairfield Police Department said in a statement on Sunday it will recommend murder charges for the alleged homicide. The actual charges will be determined by the Solano County District Attorney’s Office. Cullen allegedly called police after shooting his brother in the 2100 block of Westphalian Drive.

headlines.title: Vegetation fire makes its way into solar facility in Sonoma County
headlines.description: Firefighters were battling a vegetation fire near Highway 101 in the North Bay that Cal Fire said made its way into a solar facility Sunday. According to Cal Fire, the vegetation fire was reported near Highway 101 and San Antonio Road in Sonoma County. The fire, dubbed the Petaluma Fire, has grown to four acres and made its way into a solar facility. This is a developing story. Details may change as more information becomes available. Stay tuned for updates.

headlines.title: Carquinez Bridge, stretch of Highway 101 reopen after weekend closures
headlines.description: The Carquinez Bridge and a busy stretch of Highway 101 in San Francisco are fully open for the Monday morning commute after Caltrans completed two major weekend projects ahead of schedule. The westbound Interstate 80 span of the Carquinez Bridge, which carries traffic southbound toward the Bay Area, reopened at midnight after being closed since Friday night. Crews installed a new layer of asphalt on the bridge during the closure. Caltrans said it had been 23 years since the span received this type of work and officials hope the new pavement will last another 20 years. Caltrans also completed work early on Highway 101 near Hospital Curve in San Francisco, with all lanes reopening around 1 a.m. Monday. The highway had been reduced to two lanes in each direction over the weekend while crews performed what Caltrans described as crucial drainage improvements. The work is intended to make the section of Highway 101 less prone to flooding.

headlines.title: Skyline Watershed Ridge Trail opens, expanding Bay Area Ridge Trail network
headlines.description: The San Francisco Public Utilities Commission opened the new six-mile Skyline Watershed Ridge Trail to the public Monday, giving visitors access to a portion of the Peninsula Watershed in San Mateo County. The trail opens at 6 a.m., and a free permit is required for entry. It runs along SFPUC property parallel to Skyline Boulevard and extends south from Highway 92. It is the newest addition to the Bay Area Ridge Trail, bringing the regional network to 413 completed miles of a planned 550 miles.

headlines.title: Bay Area fire crews help fight Hawk Fire in Nevada
headlines.description: Bay Area fire crews were deployed overnight to help fight the Hawk Fire near Reno, which has spread to more than 15,000 acres. The Hawk Fire started late Saturday and grew, quickly driven by strong winds. As of Sunday evening, the blaze left six people hurt, more than 5,000 others without power and thousands affected by the evacuation orders. As 800 firefighters battle the flames, thousands are leaving or ready to go. “Currently, we have 42,000 individuals who are displaced and on an active evacuation with approximately 45,000 individuals that are in the status to be prepared to evacuate,” U.S. Forest Service Incident Commander Shane Ackerson. Authorities confirmed the fire was human-caused, but haven’t said if it was suspected as arson. Local fire agencies were mobilized by Cal OES to help on the fire lines. Overnight, a group left Oakland, two engines from different Bay Area departments and one engine and battalion chief from Oakland and San Francisco, as well. “San Francisco was called early this morning a little bit after 1 a.m. to help with fires in the Reno area, we sent two type six fire engines which are larger pickup trucks style fire engines which are more maneuverable than most of the larger fire engines that people are familiar with,” San Francisco Fire Department Capt. Mariano Elias said. The state agreement allows for fast aid while maintaining protection for California. Closer to the fire, people are trying to stay safe, watching and waiting for word. Annemarie Anaya, who used to live in the Bay Area but moved to the Reno area just over a year ago, was one of the residents who had to evacuate. “I packed what I could and we loaded both cars, like I said electricity went off so my husband had to at least get the garage open to get the car out the garage and we just headed away,” she said. “It happened so fast, the winds kicked up and it just took over, so I know that the firefighters and the officials everyone is doing what they can I just hope everyone stays safe.”

headlines.title: Young man dies after being shot in a shopping center parking lot in El Cerrito
headlines.description: A young man died after being shot in the parking lot of a shopping center in El Cerrito Sunday, according to the police department. Police said they received a call of a shooting in the parking lot of the Del Norte Plaza Shopping center, located at 11299 San Pablo Avenue, at around 12:17 p.m. There, authorities said they found a young man who had been shot in the parking lot near Los Moles Restaurant. The man died at the scene, according to police. Officials said witnesses reported the suspects were in an altercation with the victim at his car and shot him. After the shooting, police said the suspects drove away southbound on S. 56th Street in a dark colored sedan. According to police, the witnesses said one of the suspects was wearing a black mask and a black North Face brand puffy jacket. The other suspect, police said, was wearing a hat and a black Nike brand jacket. The police department asks anyone with information to contact them at 510-237-3233.

headlines.title: Abandoned railway trestle near EBMUD plant in Oakland catches fire
headlines.description: An abandoned railway trestle near the East Bay Municipal Utility District (EBMUD) caught fire Saturday night in Oakland, according to firefighters. Just after 10 p.m. on Saturday, Oakland Fire said crews were battling a fire on the old train trestles near the EBMUD plant. They had asked residents living 3 miles west of the intersection of West Grand Avenue and Wake Avenue to keep their windows and doors closed until air quality conditions could improve. Although firefighters were able to keep the fire from spreading to the building, they had to battle spot fires in the yard at the treatment plant. On Sunday, fire crews said they were cooling hot spots on the trestles and then will get heavy equipment to pull down the still smoldering infrastructure.

headlines.title: License plate reader network helps police locate missing Petaluma man 150 miles away
headlines.description: An at-risk missing adult was safely located more than 150 miles from his home after the Petaluma Police Department utilized an automated license plate reader network to track his vehicle across multiple counties. At approximately 6:38 p.m. on Aug. 21, Petaluma police received a report that a man with memory issues had left his residence earlier in the afternoon and had not returned, according to the department. Officers immediately entered him into the Missing and Unidentified Persons System (MUPS) as an at-risk missing adult and distributed his vehicle’s information to allied law enforcement agencies. During the investigation, police used the Flock Safety Automated License Plate Reader (ALPR) network to search for the vehicle. An initial detection showed the man had traveled outside of Petaluma and into Solano County. As the evening progressed, additional Flock detections captured the vehicle continuing north through Lake and Mendocino counties. Each detection provided updated location and directional data, allowing Petaluma dispatchers to alert law enforcement agencies farther north. This coordination helped responding agencies focus their resources along the man’s anticipated route. When the system indicated the vehicle was heading toward Humboldt County, Petaluma police notified the Humboldt County Sheriff’s Office and the California Highway Patrol. At approximately 11:35 p.m., Humboldt County sheriff’s deputies safely located the man and his vehicle. His family was notified so arrangements could be made for his safe return. Petaluma police noted that the incident highlights the value of ALPR technology as an investigative tool during time-sensitive public safety incidents, allowing multiple jurisdictions to connect and focus their search efforts.
